steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on EdgeGAE, an edge-aware graph autoencoder that solves the traveling salesman problem as link prediction and is trained on scale-imbalanced data. Cover routing problems and TSP, traditional solvers, neural combinatorial optimization and GNN-based methods, their drawbacks, our approach and contributions, and a paper outline.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. COPs, routing problems and TSP
2. Traditional solvers (exact solvers, heuristics, EAs) and their limits
3. Neural combinatorial optimization: early work, Pointer Networks
4. GNN-based solvers: autoregressive vs. non-autoregressive
5. Drawbacks: fixed-size training, need for large labeled imbalanced data
6. EdgeGAE: TSP as link prediction, edge-aware encoder/decoder, active sampling; contributions; paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. COPs and TSP
- COPs in many practical OR applications; most NP-hard, hard in polynomial time
- routing problems: logistics, transportation, urban planning, supply chain management
- plan route scheduling for vehicles under constraints; minimize total distance/overhead with constraints satisfied
- TSP: shortest path visiting given locations once, return to start

2. Traditional methods
- enumeration search non-trivial even with hundreds of cities
- mathematical solvers vs. hand-crafted heuristics
- Concorde: cutting-plane + branch-and-bound
- exact solvers: optimal with guarantees for small/medium; intractable for large-scale (exponential complexity)
- EAs: good for large search spaces, but many function evaluations -> huge cost; can't learn from historical data; restart from scratch after minor changes

3. NCO
- neural combinatorial optimization, data-driven optimization view
- end-to-end training, learn directly from instances instead of hand-crafted heuristics
- early: Hopfield networks, template models
- sequence-to-sequence -> Vinyals et al. Pointer Network with attention, sequential TSP tours
- Bello et al.: Pointer Network trained with Actor-Critic RL instead of supervised learning

4. GNNs
- graph representation learning -> routing as sequential decision tasks on graphs
- GNNs for COPs: routing, facility location, graph coloring
- competitive with OR solvers on small instances; fast inference -> real-time decisions
- autoregressive (one city per step) vs. non-autoregressive (one-shot, arbitrarily large graphs)
- Nowak et al.: GNN outputs adjacency matrix -> beam search
- Joshi et al.: residual gated graph ConvNet for TSP
- Fu et al.: RL instead of beam search; heatmaps -> Monte Carlo tree search

5. Drawbacks
- trained on fixed-size instances -> poor generalization to different numbers of cities
- need millions of instances with optimal solutions; in practice limited, imbalanced data (more small-scale, fewer large-scale)

6. EdgeGAE
- edge-aware graph autoencoder, learns from imbalanced data
- TSP reformulated as link prediction on the graph (not step-by-step route planning); cities = nodes, route = connections
- conventional GAE uses only node features, ignores edges; edge features (Euclidean distances) crucial
- encoder: residual gated graph convolutions -> explicit edge embeddings; edge-centered decoder (edge + node embeddings) instead of inner products
- active sampling (AS): oversampling + undersampling
- evaluated up to hundreds of cities; optimal gap, F1 score
- contributions: (1) TSP as link prediction, edge-aware GAE; (2) random active sampling for extremely imbalanced data; (3) benchmark of 50,000 instances, 50 to 500 cities, instances inversely proportional to number of cities; EdgeGAE outperforms other learning-based methods
- organization: Section II literature review; III formulation + method; IV experiments; V conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) show up in many practical applications of operational research (OR). Most COPs are NP-hard and hard to solve within polynomial time. Routing problems are an important area of research on COPs, and they come up in many application scenarios like logistics, transportation, urban planning, and supply chain management. In general, routing problems are about planning route scheduling solutions for a group of vehicles under some constraints, so that they make deliveries or provide services to a set of locations efficiently. The goal is to minimize the total traveling distance or overhead while all the constraints are satisfied. The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is one of the most studied routing problems, and it aims to find the shortest path that goes through a set of given locations once and returns to the initial location.

Since TSP is NP-hard, it is not trivial to find an efficient polynomial-time solution through enumeration search, even for TSPs with only hundreds of cities. Traditional methods for TSPs and other optimization problems can generally be split into mathematical solvers and hand-crafted heuristics. A representative exact solver is Concorde, which uses both cutting-plane and branch-and-bound approaches to solve TSPs. For small and medium-sized problems, exact TSP solvers can find optimal solutions with guarantees. But for large-scale instances it becomes intractable for exact solvers to get an exact solution in a reasonable amount of time, because the computational complexity grows exponentially. To get around this, evolutionary algorithms (EAs) are used to solve TSPs, and they have proven to be well-suited for exploring a large search space. But EAs are population-based and often need a large number of function evaluations, which leads to huge computational costs, especially when the evaluations take a long time. Also, EAs can't learn from existing historical data, and even small changes to the problem mean the search has to restart from scratch.

An alternative is neural combinatorial optimization (NCO), which the machine learning community has explored from the point of view of data-driven optimization. Instead of hand-crafted heuristics, NCO trains neural networks end-to-end to solve any combinatorial problems by learning directly from existing instances. Early work on learning-based approaches for routing problems goes back to Hopfield networks and template models. With the strong performance of sequence-to-sequence models, Vinyals et al. proposed a Pointer Network with an attention mechanism that outputs TSP tours sequentially. In similar work by Bello et al., the Pointer Network is trained with an Actor-Critic reinforcement learning strategy instead of supervised learning.

As graph representation learning developed, NP-hard routing problems have been reconsidered as sequential decision tasks on graphs. So recently there has been a surge of work training graph neural networks (GNNs) to solve COPs like routing problems, facility location problems and graph coloring problems. Compared to OR solvers, GNN-based methods have reached competitive performance on small problem instances. Once it is trained, a GNN-based solver can generate approximate optimal solutions in a very short inference time, which makes it good for real-time decision-making. End-to-end learning for TSPs can be split into autoregressive and non-autoregressive approaches, depending on how the solutions are generated. In autoregressive methods, the TSP tour is built regressively by picking one city at each step. Non-autoregressive approaches instead make predictions for arbitrarily large graphs in one shot. In an early work, Nowak et al. trained GNNs to output the prediction as an adjacency matrix of the input graph, and this is then converted into feasible solutions with beam search. Joshi et al. built on ideas from Nowak et al. and introduced the residual gated graph ConvNet to solve TSP. Extending the work of Joshi et al., Fu et al. replaced the beam search with reinforcement learning techniques. The output heatmaps are given to Monte Carlo tree search to get TSP tours.

But existing data-driven NCO approaches for TSPs have clear drawbacks. First, most learning-based solvers are trained only on TSP instances of a fixed size, and they generalize poorly to test cases where the number of cities is different from the training data. Second, training such a solver often needs millions of TSP instances with optimal solutions to get competitive performance, which assumes the model has enough labeled data to train on. But this assumption is hard to satisfy in practice, because NP-hard problems usually have a limited number of imbalanced optimized instances, with more small-scale cases and fewer large-scale cases.

In this paper we propose an edge-aware graph autoencoder (EdgeGAE) framework that solves TSPs by learning from imbalanced data. Traditional TSP solvers treat TSP as a route planning task and decide the next city to visit step by step, but this work reformulates TSP as a link prediction task on the graph. Each city is a node on the graph, and the optimal route can be represented by the connections between the nodes. The encoder-decoder structure is widely used for traditional link prediction tasks in graph representation learning. But the conventional graph autoencoder (GAE) fails on TSP tasks, because its encoding-decoding process only looks at node features and ignores how important edge information is for TSP. Since the quality of solutions to routing problems depends heavily on the edge features (i.e., Euclidean distances), we modify the encoder with residual gated graph convolutions for message passing so that it learns explicit edge embeddings in the latent space. To get around the limitation of inner products, where only nodes are involved, we design an edge-centered decoder model that uses both the edge embeddings and the corresponding node embeddings for link prediction. During training we use an active sampling (AS) strategy that combines oversampling and undersampling to handle the imbalanced distribution of the training data. The framework is evaluated on TSP instances of different sizes up to hundreds of cities and compared with state-of-the-art learning-based methods in terms of the optimal gap and the F1 score. Compared to traditional learning-based TSP solvers, the main contributions of this work are:

1. We first turn the TSP from a traditional path planning problem into a link prediction task in graph representation learning. Based on this, we redesign the structure of the vanilla graph autoencoder and propose an edge-aware graph autoencoder model that fits the characteristics of TSP.

2. We deal with the challenge of extremely imbalanced data distribution by adding a random active sampling strategy to the end-to-end training process. Using oversampling and undersampling lets our model keep strong generalization performance with only a few large-scale training samples.

3. To check model performance in scale-imbalanced optimization scenarios, we build a benchmark dataset of 50,000 TSP instances with different scales, from 50 to 500 cities. The data has an extremely imbalanced distribution where the number of instances is inversely proportional to the number of cities. Comprehensive experiments on the benchmark show that the proposed EdgeGAE outperforms other learning-based methods for solving TSPs.

The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section II reviews existing work on learning-based NCO methods for TSPs and their generalization ability. Section III gives the problem formulation and describes the proposed methodology in detail. Section IV presents the experimental results and their analysis. Section V concludes the paper and outlines future work.

steps.text:
Combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) exist in many practical applications of operational research (OR). Most COPs are NP-hard and difficult to solve within polynomial time [1]. As an important field of research on COPs, routing problems arise in various application scenarios such as logistics, transportation, urban planning, and supply chain management. Generally, routing problems involve planning route scheduling solutions for a group of vehicles under constrained conditions so as to make deliveries or provide services to a set of locations efficiently, with the target of minimizing the total traveling distance or overhead while satisfying all constraints [2]. The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is one of the most intensively studied routing problems; it aims to find the shortest path that traverses a set of given locations once and returns to the initial location.

As TSP is NP-hard, finding an efficient polynomial-time solution via enumeration search is non-trivial even for TSPs with only hundreds of cities. Traditional methods for solving TSPs and other optimization problems can be generally categorized into mathematical solvers [3,4,5] and hand-crafted heuristics [6,7,8,9]. A representative exact solver is Concorde [3], which incorporates both cutting-plane and branch-and-bound approaches for solving TSPs. For small and medium-sized problems, exact TSP solvers can find optimal solutions with guarantees. For large-scale instances, however, the exponential growth of the computational complexity makes it intractable for exact solvers to obtain an exact solution within a reasonable amount of time. To alleviate this limitation, evolutionary algorithms (EAs) have been adopted to solve TSPs and have proven well-suited for exploring a large search space. However, population-based EAs often require a large number of function evaluations, leading to huge computational costs, especially when evaluations are time-consuming. In addition, EAs are unable to learn from existing historical data, and even minor modifications to the problem require restarting the search from scratch.

An alternative, known as neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) [10,1], has been explored in the machine learning community from the perspective of data-driven optimization [11,12,1]. Instead of relying on hand-crafted heuristics, NCO trains neural networks in an end-to-end manner to solve combinatorial problems by learning directly from existing instances. Early work on learning-based approaches for routing problems can be traced back to Hopfield networks [13] and template models [14]. Following the compelling performance of sequence-to-sequence models [15,16], Vinyals et al. proposed a Pointer Network [17] with an attention mechanism [18] to output TSP tours sequentially. In similar work by Bello et al. [10], the Pointer Network is trained with an Actor-Critic reinforcement learning strategy instead of supervised learning [17].

With the development of graph representation learning [19,20,21], NP-hard routing problems have been reconsidered as sequential decision tasks on graphs [22]. As a result, there has been a recent surge of work on training graph neural networks (GNNs) [23,24,25] to solve COPs such as routing problems [26,22,27], facility location problems [28] and graph coloring problems [29]. GNN-based methods have achieved competitive performance compared to OR solvers on small problem instances [27,22,30,31]. Once trained, a GNN-based solver can generate approximate optimal solutions in a very short inference time, which makes it favorable for real-time decision-making. Depending on how solutions are generated, end-to-end learning for TSPs can be categorized into autoregressive and non-autoregressive approaches. In autoregressive methods, a TSP tour is constructed regressively by identifying one city at each step [30,10,32,33]. Non-autoregressive approaches, by contrast, make predictions for arbitrarily large graphs in a one-shot fashion [26,22,34,27]. In an early work [26], Nowak et al. trained GNNs to output the prediction as an adjacency matrix of the input graph, which is then converted into feasible solutions by beam search. Joshi et al. [22] built on ideas from [26] and introduced the residual gated graph ConvNet [35] for solving TSP. Extending the work in [22], Fu et al. [36] replaced beam search with reinforcement learning techniques, feeding the output heatmaps into Monte Carlo tree search to obtain TSP tours.

However, existing data-driven NCO approaches for TSPs suffer from distinct drawbacks. First, most learning-based solvers are trained only on fixed-sized TSP instances [33,32,22,17] and exhibit poor generalization to test cases whose number of cities differs from that of the training data [27]. Second, training such a solver often requires millions of TSP instances with optimal solutions to achieve competitive performance, which assumes that the model has sufficient labeled training data. This assumption is non-trivial to satisfy in practice, since NP-hard problems usually have a limited number of imbalanced optimized instances, containing more small-scale cases and fewer large-scale cases.

In this paper, we propose an edge-aware graph autoencoder (EdgeGAE) framework for solving TSPs by learning from imbalanced data. Unlike traditional TSP solvers, which treat TSP as a route planning task and decide the next city to visit step by step, this work reformulates TSP as a link prediction task on the graph. Each city is treated as a node, and the optimal route can be represented by the connections between nodes. The encoder-decoder structure is widely adopted for traditional link prediction tasks in graph representation learning. However, the conventional graph autoencoder (GAE) fails to solve TSP tasks, as its encoding-decoding process considers only node features and overlooks the importance of edge information for TSP. Since the quality of solutions to routing problems relies heavily on edge features (i.e., Euclidean distances), we modify the encoder with residual gated graph convolutions for message passing in order to learn explicit edge embeddings in the latent space. To alleviate the limitation of inner products, which involve only nodes, we design an edge-centered decoder that incorporates both the edge and the corresponding node embeddings for link prediction. During training, we adopt an active sampling (AS) strategy that incorporates oversampling and undersampling to deal with the imbalanced distribution of the training data. The proposed framework is evaluated on TSP instances of different sizes up to hundreds of cities and compared with state-of-the-art learning-based methods in terms of the optimal gap and the F1 score. Compared with traditional learning-based TSP solvers, the main contributions of this work are as follows:

1. We first transform the TSP from a traditional path planning problem into a link prediction task in graph representation learning. Building on this, we redesign the structure of the vanilla graph autoencoder and propose an edge-aware graph autoencoder model that accommodates the characteristics of TSP.

2. We address the challenge of extremely imbalanced data distribution by introducing a random active sampling strategy into the end-to-end training process. Incorporating oversampling and undersampling enables our model to retain strong generalization performance with only a few large-scale training samples.

3. To validate model performance in scale-imbalanced optimization scenarios, we construct a benchmark dataset of 50,000 TSP instances with varying scales, ranging from 50 to 500 cities. The data follows an extremely imbalanced distribution in which the number of instances is inversely proportional to the number of cities. Comprehensive experiments on this benchmark demonstrate that the proposed EdgeGAE outperforms other learning-based methods for solving TSPs.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section II reviews existing work on learning-based NCO methods for TSPs and their generalization ability. Section III provides the problem formulation and describes the proposed methodology in detail. Section IV presents the experimental results and their analysis. Section V concludes the paper and outlines future work.
